newsitem.title: PERU: No guerrilla prisoners to be freed, Fujimori vows.
newsitem.headline: No guerrilla prisoners to be freed, Fujimori vows.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori on Thursday vehemently denied his government would free jailed Marxist rebels in a deal to end the 93-day hostage standoff at the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima.

"I absolutely, totally and flatly deny that my government's position has changed," Fujimori said, referring to reports he might free some Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) detainees in order to end the siege.
"My government's position remains the same. There will be no freeing of MRTA prisoners," he said on local Radioprogramas del Peru in a broadcast interview from the central Andes.

Lima has been rife with speculation that Fujimori agreed at a meeting this week with Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to free MRTA prisoners to win the release of 72 dignitaries being held by about 20 MRTA rebels.
"The security of the country comes before any other interest. I'm sorry if that sounds hard," said Fujimori.
MRTA is demanding release of about 450 jailed comrades in exchange for freeing the hostages, held in the Japanese residence since Dec. 17.

Fujimori has consistently rejected that demand. But he is believed to be considering some concessions such as improving notoriously harsh prison conditions for rebels convicted of terrorism, or release of a small member of MRTA rebels not yet sentenced or convicted on lesser charges.

In a sign of progress toward ending the siege peacefully, Cuba confirmed on Thursday it had accepted a request from Japan to grant asylum to the hostage-takers if that would contribute to ending the crisis and if all sides agreed.
In Havana, the ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma said Komura delivered Japan's formal request in a meeting late on Wednesday with President Fidel Castro.
"The Cuban government ratified its willingess to cooperate where possible in the solution to the situation, on the basis of an agreement between the involved parties," Granma said.

An MRTA spokesman said on Thursday the group had no comment on the asylum request -- a possibly significant change, since the movement in the past has poured cold water on the idea of asylum in a third country in exchange for freeing the hostages.
"For the moment we have no statement on that issue," an MRTA spokesman inside the besieged house said in a radio communication with reporters when asked about Cuban asylum.
Komura later arrived in the Dominican Republic, which like Cuba has also offered asylum to some of the hostage-takers.

Fujimori, whose popularity has rested largely on his tough line with guerrillas, said any release of MRTA prisoners would set a dangerous precedent for a country ravaged by violence since 1980 by MRTA and a Maoist group, the Shining Path.
"We cannot backslide here because this may generate other cases in which I am asked to free prisoners, including other terrorist groups or common criminals," said Fujimori.

"Perhaps for other countries, this might not have so much meaning and they may seek solutions that don't take this into account, but we Peruvians have suffered for 15 years and we've had 25,000 deaths," he said.

As a three-man mediation panel has been talking with both sides, Fujimori's army said this week it arrested 38 "MRTA terrorists" and seized weapons in sweeps through rebel strongholds in the eastern Andean foothills.
The MRTA spokesman denied that the 38 detainees belonged to the organisation, calling them "defenseless peasants" picked up in "arbitrary and indiscriminate" roundups.
But while criticising the army sweeps, he signalled MRTA remained willing to keep negotiating on the hostages and that the army offensive need not pose an unsurmountable obstacle.

Two members of the mediation panel, Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, met with the guerrillas inside the residence for about two hours late on Thursday, but they did not comment. The two sides have met face-to-face only once in two weeks.

Through one of the house's windows, journalists could see a group of hostages gathered around a candle and singing on Thursday evening. The gathering might have been a birthday celebration for Minnig, who turned 45.
